title: DNA-CIM: DNA Sequence Analysis Using RRAM-Based Compute In-Memory Accelerator
problem: DNA sequence matching and mutation analysis are computationally intensive tasks causing memory wall problems in conventional CPU/GPU architectures. Large genomic datasets require frequent off-chip memory access, limiting throughput and energy efficiency.
motivation: Genomics applications (disorder identification, evolutionary analysis, mutation characterization) require efficient processing of massive sequence datasets. Compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures can eliminate memory-processor bottleneck by performing operations directly in storage.
method: DNA sequences are converted to binary numbers (0s and 1s) and compared using fast bitwise logic operations (XOR and AND operations, which identify matching and different bits) performed directly inside resistive memory rather than the CPU. Specialized circuits detect the results in-memory without moving data, and mutation classification—identifying where sequences differ—happens at the memory level. The architecture was designed and verified through simulation at 65-nanometer technology.
key_novelty: This is the first system combining in-memory bitwise DNA comparisons (using resistive memory to perform logical operations on individual bits) with nearby mutation classification, avoiding the slow data transfers to the processor that limit conventional approaches.
contributions: DNA-to-binary conversion enabling in-memory XOR/AND operations
RRAM macro + MLSC for efficient bitwise sequence alignment
2.042 TCUPS/W energy efficiency (teracups = tera comparisons per unit)
Addresses architecture variability challenges in RRAM
limitations: 65nm technology node outdated; scaling to modern processes (28nm, 7nm) not discussed
RRAM variability only partially addressed; reliability under process corners not thoroughly characterized
Simulation-only results; no silicon implementation or experimental validation
Limited to binary sequence representation; extensibility to quality scores, alignments, or other metadata unclear
Mutation analysis limited to classification; no detailed error analysis or sensitivity characterization
No comparison with state-of-the-art GPU/FPGA baselines in terms of performance-per-watt
Memory capacity and scalability to realistic genome sizes not specified
